title: Zephaniah 3:14–20
context: Zephaniah 3:14–20 is a closing song of joy. The prophet calls the daughter of Zion to sing and rejoice, because the LORD has taken away her judgments and thrown out her enemy; the King of Israel, the LORD, is among her, and she will no longer fear evil. In that day Jerusalem will hear, "Don’t be afraid, Zion," for the LORD her God is among her, a mighty one who saves, who rejoices over her with singing and calms her in his love. The LORD then speaks directly, promising to deal with her oppressors, save the lame, gather the scattered, and give them praise and honor among all peoples when he restores their fortunes. Shared ground: both traditions receive the LORD’s presence among his people, his saving power, and his delight in them as common ground, read in light of the return from exile and of God’s final restoration in Christ, without drawing a tradition-specific contrast from the song.

verses.text: Sing, daughter of Zion! Shout, Israel! Be glad and rejoice with all your heart, daughter of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Zephaniah calls the daughter of Zion to sing, shout, and rejoice with all her heart. Arminian readers see joy as the right response to God’s saving work, calling his people to celebrate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the call to rejoice as grounded in what God has done. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and read the song as the turning point of the book.

verses.text: The LORD has taken away your judgments. He has thrown out your enemy. The King of Israel, the LORD, is among you. You will not be afraid of evil any more.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the LORD has taken away her judgments, thrown out her enemy, and the King of Israel, the LORD, is among her. Arminians see God removing both punishment and enemies, so his people need no longer fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s kingship and presence as the source of salvation. Both traditions hold this as shared ground, and they read the LORD among his people as the heart of the promise.

verses.text: In that day, it will be said to Jerusalem, “Don’t be afraid, Zion. Don’t let your hands be weak.”
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says that on that day Jerusalem will be told not to fear or let her hands be weak. Arminian readers see God’s encouragement to his people, strengthening them to live without fear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s word of comfort as rooted in his presence. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and compare similar words of encouragement in Isaiah 35:3–4 by reference.

verses.text: The LORD, your God, is among you, a mighty one who will save. He will rejoice over you with joy. He will calm you in his love. He will rejoice over you with singing.
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet says the LORD her God is among her, a mighty one who saves, rejoicing over her with joy and singing and calming her in his love. Arminians see God’s delight in his people as a powerful encouragement to trust him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s saving love as the foundation of his people’s joy. Both traditions hold this verse as shared ground, and they read God’s singing over his people as a picture of his delight.

verses.text: I will remove those who grieve about the appointed feasts from you. They are a burden and a reproach to you.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will remove those who grieve over the appointed feasts, who are a burden and reproach. Arminian readers see God ending the sorrow of those cut off from worship in exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s restoring work. Both traditions note that this verse is difficult in Hebrew and translated in different ways, and they hold its details loosely.

verses.text: Behold, at that time I will deal with all those who afflict you; and I will save those who are lame and gather those who were driven away. I will give them praise and honor, whose shame has been in all the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will deal with those who afflict them, save the lame, gather the scattered, and give them praise and honor. Arminians see God lifting up the weak and outcast, turning shame into honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s gracious reversal for his people. Both traditions compare Micah 4:6–7 by reference, and they hold this as shared ground.

verses.text: At that time I will bring you in, and at that time I will gather you; for I will give you honor and praise among all the peoples of the earth when I restore your fortunes before your eyes, says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will bring them in, gather them, and give them honor among all peoples when he restores their fortunes before their eyes. Arminian readers see God’s promise of restoration as a hope that sustains faithful people through judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sure purpose to restore his people. Both traditions read the promise in light of the return from exile and of final restoration, and they hold this as shared ground.
